cover.headline: A fertiliser and chemicals PSU priced at the value of its share portfolio, as it always has been
cover.lead: GSFC makes fertilisers (78% of FY26 revenue: ammonium sulphate, APS, urea, DAP and traded products) and industrial chemicals (22%: caprolactam, nylon-6, melamine), and owns shares in other Gujarat companies worth ~₹5,364 cr: **89% of its ₹6,009 cr market value at the 30-Sep-2026 close** (listed stakes alone 62%). Q1FY27 showed both businesses at the mercy of outside prices: revenue +64%, but the fertiliser EBIT margin fell to 4.1% (8.5%) as sulphur, ammonia and P₂O₅ spiked, while industrial products earned ₹116 cr of EBIT (₹25 cr) on a $816/t caprolactam spread. Coverage is effectively nil; the last full broker series (Emkay) used a sum of the parts, and so do we: **the business at 6x Sep-27E EBITDA, the holdings at market, plus net cash, less a 41% holding discount**, GSFC's own median since 2021 in quarters with normal earnings. That gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with HOLD.** P/E (₹148) and DCF (₹196, holdings at full book) bracket it. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: The market has never paid for the business
arguments.p: Since June 2021 GSFC's market value has been a median 1.6x its listed holdings. Take the holdings at market and the cash at face value, and the price has implied roughly nothing for a business that earned ₹514-1,588 cr of EBITDA a year (median -0.3x EBITDA). On our look-through measure (business at 6x EBITDA) the discount has ranged from 20% to 72%. On 30-Sep-2026 it was ~47%: cheap on assets (0.49x book), not cheap against its own history.

arguments.h: Fertiliser margins are set by policy and sulphur
arguments.p: Urea (New Urea Policy) and DAP (special package: import parity plus 4%) are protected. GSFC's largest manufactured products, APS and ammonium sulphate, are not: they run on sulphur, which averaged ~₹82,000/t in Q1FY27 and was above ₹115,000/t by mid-August. Rabi 2026-27 NBS rates were not announced by 30-Sep. We model a fertiliser EBITDA margin of 5.0% / 6.5% / 7.0% (FY27-29E) vs 6.6% in FY26 and 17.6% in the FY23 boom.

arguments.h: Chemicals: a crisis windfall, not a trend
arguments.p: Industrial products EBIT went from ₹56 cr (FY25) to ₹200 cr (FY26) and ₹116 cr in Q1FY27 alone, as China curbed exports and the capro-benzene spread jumped to $816/t (FY26 average $535). Management expects the spread to be "stable to soft"; melamine output has already stopped on Chinese imports. We model a 13.5% EBITDA margin in FY27 falling to 11% (FY19-26 average ~10%).

ROE was 5.5% in FY26. The portfolio has never been sold or distributed; the payout is ~30% of profit (~1.6% of net worth) against a state policy floor of 5% of net worth (the policy allows less with Finance Department approval, e.g. for capex); no buyback is planned. A new capex cycle (Sikka acid plants, Dahej complex) starts without a disclosed cost, under a board that had three managing directors in FY26. Until that changes, we see no reason for the discount to close.

catalysts: Rabi 2026-27 NBS subsidy rates (due for the October-March season): the main swing factor for APS, AS and NPK margins in H2FY27.
Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): the first quarter with sulphur above ₹1 lakh/t; working capital and borrowings.
Award and cost of the Sikka phosphoric/sulphuric acid EPC contract (expected by Sep-2026, not announced by 30-Sep) and the Dahej plan.
Commissioning of the C-Train modification at Sikka (APS or DAP on one train; due in Q2FY27).
Any dividend, buyback or stake sale under Gujarat's 2023 PSU capital policy: the one thing that would narrow the holding discount.

sections.title: Two commodity businesses on one integrated site, plus a portfolio of shares

blocks.p: State-promoted (Government of Gujarat, through Gujarat State Investments Ltd, 37.84%) maker of fertilisers and industrial chemicals, incorporated 1962 as India's first joint-sector fertiliser company. Two complexes: Fertilizernagar, Vadodara (ammonia, urea, ammonium sulphate, APS, sulphuric acid, caprolactam, nylon-6, melamine, methanol, MEK oxime, HX crystal) and Sikka, Jamnagar (DAP/APS trains, own jetty and ammonia storage used for imports). Plus GSFC Agrotech (distribution subsidiary), a 99-year lease on 276.7 ha at Dahej (Nov-2025) and a large portfolio of shares in other Gujarat PSUs. Fertilizer products (78% of FY26 revenue): urea (3.25 lakh t sold), ammonium sulphate (5.76 lakh t, record), APS 20:20:0:13 (7.16 lakh t, record), DAP (1.46 lakh t), NPK, plus traded urea (3.20 lakh t) and P&K (1.43 lakh t). Industrial products (22%): caprolactam (54,671 t sold externally; the rest goes into nylon-6), nylon-6 (35,010 t), melamine (38,780 t), methanol, MEK oxime, HX crystal, technical-grade urea and traded ammonia.

blocks.p: **Fertilisers are a policy-priced conversion business.** GSFC makes ammonia from piped natural gas, sulphuric acid from sulphur, and buys phosphoric acid (P₂O₅) and rock. Urea earns a fixed return under the New Urea Policy: the subsidy covers the gap between cost (including gas) and the fixed farm price, so gas costs pass through. DAP, APS, AS and NPK get a fixed subsidy per kg of nutrient (NBS), reset each season; MRPs are nominally free but farmers' ability to pay caps them, so when sulphur or P₂O₅ jump faster than the subsidy, margins shrink. In the current crisis the government added a DAP special package (import parity plus 4%). GSFC also trades imported urea, DAP and NPK at thin margins. **Industrial products are commodity chemicals**: caprolactam (from benzene) goes into nylon-6 (sold as chips and engineering plastics), melamine (from urea) into laminates. Prices follow China, the world's swing producer; the capro-benzene spread is the profit driver.

sections.title: Fertilisers run on subsidy tables; caprolactam and melamine run on China

blocks.p: India sold a record 708.9 lakh t of fertilisers in FY26 (+2%): urea 396 lakh t, DAP ~94 lakh t, SSP 55 lakh t, with imports filling the gap (DAP +37% to 62.5 lakh t). For a producer like GSFC three things matter. **First, policy sets the price.** Urea is fully controlled (New Urea Policy: cost-plus, gas passed through). P&K fertilisers get a fixed subsidy per kg of nutrient (NBS) that the government resets every kharif and rabi season; in a cost spike it decides how much the industry absorbs. **Second, inputs are imported and volatile.** Sulphur rose 164% in FY26 (average $376/t) and spiked again in Q1FY27; P₂O₅ reached $1,700/t. **Third, for chemicals, China is the price setter**: caprolactam, nylon-6 chips and melamine prices fell 10-21% in FY26 on Chinese oversupply, then jumped in Q1FY27 when China curbed exports during the Middle East crisis.

bullets: **Volumes are at records, profits are not.** Sales of 22.31 lakh t in FY26 (+12%; manufactured 17.68 lakh t, traded 4.63 lakh t); AS (5.76 lakh t) and APS (7.16 lakh t) were the highest ever. Q1FY27 5.26 lakh t (+17%), with traded P&K 1.31 lakh t. FY27 budget: "more than 22 lakh MT".

**What is protected, what is not.** Urea (3.25 lakh t sold) earns a regulated return with gas passed through; DAP has the special package. APS and AS, nearly three-quarters of manufactured sales, use sulphuric acid: with sulphur at ~₹82,000/t (Q1 average) rising above ₹1.15 lakh/t, management called them "a real uncomfort" and imported AS rather than make it.

**Subsidy and cash.** Subsidy income ₹4,514 cr (41% of group revenue) in FY26; receivable ₹1,453 cr at Mar-26 and ~₹500 cr outstanding in August (dues received to the third week of July). The DAP package pays ~6 months after sale, which is why GSFC borrowed in Q1FY27.

pair.title: Sales mix: AS and APS dominate
Our forecast: fertiliser EBITDA back to ~₹770 cr by FY29E

blocks.callout: **Our view:** a competent operator with no pricing power. We model revenue +35% / -8% / +4% (FY27-29E: price up, then easing) and EBITDA margin 5.0% / 6.5% / 7.0%. Every 1 point of fertiliser margin moves FY28E EPS by ~₹2.0 (13%). The Sikka acid plant would cut the sulphur and P₂O₅ exposure, but not before FY29.

pair.title: IP EBITDA margin: 1% to 21% and back
IP EBIT by quarter: ₹116 cr in Q1FY27

bullets: **Products.** Caprolactam (~0.8 lakh t produced a year, ~55,000 t sold outside, the rest into nylon-6), nylon-6 chips and compounds (35,010 t sold in FY26), melamine (38,780 t), methanol, MEK oxime, HX crystal (new 20 TPD plant from Oct-2024), technical-grade urea and traded ammonia (imported through the Sikka jetty).
**FY26: best EBIT in four years (₹200 cr)** on technical urea, HX crystal, traded ammonia and melamine exports, despite lower caprolactam and nylon realisations (spread $535/t vs $578/t).

**Q1FY27: revenue ₹635 cr (+15%), EBIT ₹116 cr (₹25 cr)** as the spread jumped to $816/t ($540/t) after China curbed exports. Melamine output was nil: cheap Chinese imports and a 38% higher gas price; GSFC has asked for anti-dumping duty.
**Outlook (management, Aug-2026):** spread "stable to soft"; melamine demand to improve; HX crystal exports steady.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the FY26-Q1FY27 profit jump is a cyclical windfall. Over FY19-26 the segment averaged a ~10% EBITDA margin with a range of 1-21%, and nothing about GSFC's capacity or costs has changed. We model revenue +10% / +2% / +4% and EBITDA margin 13.5% / 11.0% / 11.0% (FY27-29E). Each point of IP margin is worth ~₹0.5 of FY28E EPS.

sections.title: The share portfolio: ~₹5,364 cr, 89% of the market value

blocks.p: GSFC owns shares in other state-linked companies, built up over decades and never sold. At the 30-Sep-2026 closes the listed holdings were worth ₹3,708 cr (₹93 a share) and the unlisted ones ₹1,656 cr at the company's March valuation. They pay dividends (₹106 cr in FY26; ~₹130 cr expected in FY27 on GNFC's ₹21 and Gujarat Energy's ₹8.90 per share) but price changes never reach the P&L: they go to reserves through OCI. The listed portfolio rose ~26% between 31-Mar and 30-Sep 2026 (GNFC +65%) while GSFC's own share price rose 8%.

blocks.callout: **Why it matters and why it does not.** The holdings make GSFC look very cheap: its whole market value is about what the shares alone are worth. But the shares are stakes in sister state companies held for strategic reasons; GSFC has never sold one by choice (the GNFC shares it gave up went into GNFC's own buyback), selling would attract capital-gains tax on large unrealised gains, and the dividends they pay (~2.4% of their value) are modest. To a minority shareholder of GSFC they are worth only what GSFC chooses to pass on. That is the holding discount, and we value it explicitly in the SOTP.

sections.title: Competitive advantage: integration and a balance sheet, but no moat in the products

verdicts: One of only two Indian caprolactam producers (with FACT); ~0.8 lakh t a year integrated into nylon-6. But price is set by Chinese imports.
Gas-based ammonia, four sulphuric acid plants (steam for the complex), own jetty and ammonia storage at Sikka; the SA-V plant (Jan-2026) and the planned Sikka phosphoric acid plant extend it.
Vintage plants (Urea-II revamped in 2025); no captive rock or phosphoric acid; buys sulphur from refiners at market prices.
Urea and DAP economics set by the government; APS/AS/NPK MRPs capped by farmer affordability; chemicals by China.
Strong in Gujarat and western India through GSFC Agrotech and cooperative channels; record AS and APS volumes in FY26; no national franchise like Coromandel.
No long-term debt; ~₹5,400 cr of shares in other companies (30-Sep-2026 prices for the listed part) and ₹1,160 cr of deposits at Mar-26.
ROE 5% in FY26; Karnalyte (impaired) and TIFERT (nil) write-offs; the portfolio is never sold; payout ~30% of profit, below the state policy's 5%-of-net-worth floor.

blocks.title: Moat scorecard
blocks.source: GAM research compilation (annual reports and calls to Sep-2026)

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict: no moat.** GSFC has real operating assets: an integrated Vadodara complex where ammonia, sulphuric acid, steam and caprolactam feed each other, a jetty at Sikka that lets it import ammonia and DAP cheaply, and one of only two caprolactam plants in India. It has a strong balance sheet. None of this gives it pricing power: the government sets the economics of urea and DAP, farmers' budgets cap APS and AS, and China sets caprolactam, nylon and melamine prices. Returns show it: ROE of ~5% (4.6-5.5% in FY24-26) outside the FY22-23 boom. What GSFC owns is a cyclical business and a portfolio, not a franchise.

sections.title: Revenue doubled in eleven years; profit only moves when a boom arrives

blocks.p: GSFC's revenue rose from ₹5,311 cr in FY15 to ₹10,946 cr in FY26, but most of that is fertiliser prices and subsidy, not volume: manufactured fertiliser sales were 16.0 lakh t in FY19 and 17.7 lakh t in FY26. Profit has had one good spell. In FY22-23 a global price boom lifted EBITDA to ₹1,321-1,588 cr and net profit to ₹1,266 cr (EPS ₹31.8). Outside that spell net profit has been ₹410-675 cr a year (₹110 cr in FY20, when industrial products lost ₹69 cr at the EBIT level), and FY26's ₹673 cr (EPS ₹16.9) is 65% above FY15's ₹409 cr: 4.6% a year. EBITDA margin was 7.2% in FY26. Other income (dividends from the share portfolio and interest) was ₹287 cr, a third of profit before tax. Q1FY27: revenue +64% to ₹3,583 cr on the Middle East price shock, PAT +14% to ₹159 cr.

pair.title: Revenue: price-driven, peaked in FY23
Net profit: one boom (FY22-23), otherwise ₹450-675 cr
EBITDA margin: 14-15% in the boom, ~7% now
Other income is a third of pre-tax profit

blocks.callout: **Our view:** GSFC is a commodity producer whose margins are set by two outside forces: the government's subsidy tables for fertilisers and Chinese supply for caprolactam, nylon and melamine. When both line up (FY22-23) profit doubles; when they do not, the business earns a mid-single-digit return on its capital and the dividend and interest income from the portfolio does much of the work.

sections.title: Profits have not turned into cash since FY24, and a new capex cycle is starting

blocks.p: In FY19-22 GSFC generated ₹2,520 cr of operating cash (helped by a ₹1,054 cr working-capital release in FY21), spent ₹784 cr on plants and cut borrowings from ₹1,559 cr (Mar-20) to ₹6 cr (Mar-22). In FY23-26 it earned ₹3,094 cr of profit but only ₹875 cr of operating cash, because subsidy receivables, inventory and traded stock rose; capex was ₹1,070 cr (Urea-II revamp, SA-V acid plant, solar) and dividends ₹855 cr. The cash pile peaked at ~₹2,300 cr net (Mar-24) and was ₹1,333 cr at Mar-26; at Jun-26 GSFC had borrowed ~₹500 cr. ROCE has been 6-7% since FY24.

blocks.callout: **The next test:** management plans a 600 TPD phosphoric acid and 1,800 TPD sulphuric acid complex at Sikka (EPC award expected by Sep-2026, cost not disclosed) and an integrated complex on 276.7 ha at Dahej (configuration stage). We pencil in ₹400 cr of capex in FY27 and ₹800 cr a year in FY28-29. Nothing in GSFC's record says these projects will earn more than the 6-7% the existing assets do; backward integration into acid is logical (it removes the sulphur and P₂O₅ exposure that crushed Q1FY27 margins), but the returns depend on world prices when the plants start.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean books, but a third of profit comes from the portfolio and cash conversion is weak

bullets: **Other income is a third of pre-tax profit.** ₹287 cr in FY26 (Screener; ₹276 cr in the AR plus ~₹11 cr associates): interest ₹143 cr (mostly on deposits that were spent on working capital in Q1FY27) and dividends ₹106 cr. Operating EBITDA was ₹790 cr. As the deposits are used, interest income falls: we model ₹235 cr of other income in FY27E.

**Fair-value accounting keeps portfolio gains out of profit.** Listed and unlisted shares are at fair value through OCI. Indian Potash (unlisted) was revalued from ₹723 cr to ₹1,275 cr in FY26 on a level-3 valuation; reserves move with GNFC and Gujarat Energy prices. Book value (₹308 a share) therefore swings with markets.

**Subsidy is 41% of revenue.** ₹4,514 cr of subsidy income in FY26, recognised at notified rates; the receivable (₹1,453 cr at Mar-26) is a key audit matter. Delays in payment show up as borrowings, as in Q1FY27.

**Profit has not turned into cash since FY24.** Operating cash −₹268 cr (FY24), ₹83 cr (FY25) and ₹136 cr (FY26) against profit of ₹564-673 cr, as subsidy receivables, inventory and traded stock rose.
**Contingent liabilities jumped.** "Other" claims not acknowledged as debt rose from ₹765 cr to ₹1,333 cr in FY26 with no breakdown in the notes; ~11% of net worth.

**Past write-offs.** Karnalyte Resources (Canadian potash, impaired ₹36 cr of ₹60 cr) and TIFERT (Tunisia, carried at nil, shares pledged to its lenders): GSFC's record on investing outside Gujarat is poor.
**Definitions.** Screener EBITDA (₹790 cr FY26) excludes other income; the company's "operating EBITDA" (₹781 cr standalone) is on the same basis. Segment results include ~₹24 cr of other income.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** The audit is clean and the definitions are standard. But profit leans on portfolio dividends and interest, the unlisted holdings are valued by the company, subsidy income is a policy number paid with a lag, contingent claims rose 74% without explanation, and three years of weak cash conversion mean reported profit has overstated the cash available to shareholders.

sections.title: A balance sheet made of shares in other companies

blocks.p: Net worth was ₹12,266 cr at Mar-2026 (₹308 a share, twice the share price). ₹4,610 cr of it is shares in other companies, carried at fair value (listed shares at the March price, unlisted ones such as Indian Potash at the company's valuation); price moves go to reserves, not profit, which is why reserves swing (₹11,693 cr at Mar-22, ₹12,059 cr at Mar-25). Operating cash: ₹200 cr of cash and bank plus ₹1,160 cr of deposits with financial institutions, against ₹27 cr of debt: net cash of ~₹1,333 cr. Working capital is driven by subsidy and stock: government subsidy receivable ₹1,453 cr and inventory ₹1,879 cr at Mar-26 (₹1,087 cr and ₹1,479 cr a year earlier). In Q1FY27 the DAP special package (paid ~6 months after sale) and rabi stocking took the company to ~₹500 cr of borrowings.

blocks.callout: **What the model does with cash:** the engine treats cash, deposits and the ₹4,610 cr investment book as one "treasury" figure and holds the investments at book. Excluding the investments, we expect net cash of ~₹769 cr at Mar-27E and ~₹688 cr at Mar-29E (₹1,333 cr at Mar-26) as working capital absorbs ~₹830 cr in FY27 and the Sikka project begins. The engine keeps working capital at the Mar-26 ratio (25.6% of revenue): we leave it there because subsidy receivables, which drive it, were rising, not falling, at Jun-26.

sections.title: Ownership: the Gujarat government controls it; foreign funds have left

blocks.p: The Government of Gujarat controls GSFC through Gujarat State Investments Ltd (37.84%, unchanged, no pledge); a further 5.65% sits in a government category. Foreign investors have been sellers: FIIs held 19.82% in Dec-2023 and 12.36% in Jun-2026, while the number of shareholders rose from 1.98 lakh to 2.99 lakh. Indian small-cap funds are the largest outside holders: Quant Small Cap Fund 3.43% and ICICI Prudential Small Cap 1.67% at Jun-2026. Retail shareholders now number ~3 lakh.

blocks.callout: **No street numbers to compare with.** We found no broker estimate for FY27-29 dated by 30-Sep-2026 (one aggregator shows a single unnamed analyst expecting FY27 profit to fall ~33%, undated). sections.title: The street: effectively no coverage since 2019

blocks.p: Coverage is effectively nil. We found no broker note on GSFC dated between July and September 2026, and no dated FY27-28 consensus. The last full research series we could find is Emkay's (2018-19), which valued GSFC on a sum of the parts; IIFL kept an ADD with a ₹140 target in April 2023 (method not given). One aggregator (Trendlyne, accessed after 30-Sep-2026) shows a single analyst with a ₹160 target and FY27 profit -32.5%, but gives no broker name or date, so we do not treat it as standing on 30-Sep-2026.

blocks.p: No broker publishes regular research on GSFC. The last full series (Emkay, 2018-19) valued it as a **sum of the parts**: the operating business on a multiple plus the investments at a discount. That is also how the stock trades: its market value has followed its holdings for five years. We use the same method, with every input dated to 30-Sep-2026.

sections.title: Our honest summary: cheap on assets, fairly priced on its own history

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** a state-run maker of ammonium sulphate, APS, urea, DAP, caprolactam, nylon-6 and melamine whose margins are set by subsidy tables and Chinese prices, plus ~₹5,364 cr of shares in GNFC, Gujarat Energy, GSPL Transmission, GIPCL, Indian Potash and others, and little debt. EPS has been ₹14-17 outside the FY22-23 boom; ROE ~5%.

**What you are paying:** ₹6,009 cr, about 89% of the value of the holdings alone, 0.49x book and 9.4x our FY28E EPS. That looks like a bargain, but GSFC has traded this way for five years: the discount to look-through value was ~47% on 30-Sep against a 41% median in normal years. On the street's method with our inputs the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}).

sections.title: Annotated financials
Glossary

exhibit.title: Terms used in this report
head: Term
What it means
rows: Ammonium sulphate (21% N, 24% S) and ammonium phosphate sulphate (20:20:0:13), GSFC's two biggest products; both need sulphuric acid, made from sulphur.
Di-ammonium phosphate (18% N, 46% P₂O₅) and urea (46% N), India's most used fertilisers; their farm prices are effectively fixed by the government.
Nutrient Based Subsidy: a fixed subsidy per kg of N, P, K and S in P&K fertilisers, reset each kharif (Apr-Sep) and rabi (Oct-Mar) season.
The urea subsidy regime: the government pays the gap between a plant's assessed cost (incl. gas) and the fixed farm price.
Extra support during the 2026 crisis that compensates DAP at import parity plus a 4% margin.
The phosphate input for DAP and APS, mostly imported; priced per tonne of P₂O₅.
Caprolactam is made from benzene and polymerised into nylon-6 (fibres, engineering plastics). The capro-benzene spread is the price gap between the two, per tonne.
A urea-based chemical used in laminates and plywood resins.
What GSFC's parts are worth added up: the business at a multiple, the holdings at market or book, plus net cash.
How far below its look-through value the market prices a company that holds shares it does not sell or pass on.
Sum of the parts: valuing each business and holding separately and adding them up.
Fair value through other comprehensive income: investments marked to market through reserves, not the P&L.
Enterprise value ÷ EBITDA; price ÷ earnings per share; price ÷ book value per share.
Discounted cash flow; Ke is the cost of equity (here 12.5% = 6.5% risk-free + 1.0 × 6% equity risk premium).
Public-sector undertaking: a company controlled by the central or a state government.
